summary: This document specifies the behavior of the UPnP Internet Gateway Device - Port Control Protocol Interworking Function (IGD-PCP IWF). It is meant to be embedded in customer premises routers so that NAT can be controlled transparently where UPnP IGD is used on the LAN side and PCP on the external side.

plainLanguage.summary: Home gadgets ask the router to open doors in one language and the provider speaks another. This is a translator between the two.

questions: how upnp port mapping works with pcp
what is upnp igd pcp interworking function
how does upnp map to pcp
how are pcp errors mapped to upnp errors
subtitle: A translator inside a home router that turns UPnP port-mapping requests into PCP requests for the provider's NAT.

tldr.problem: Home devices ask the router to open ports using UPnP IGD, but when the provider runs a Carrier Grade NAT that is controlled with PCP, a UPnP mapping alone would give an external address and port that cannot be used beyond the provider NAT.
tldr.mechanism: An interworking function (IGD-PCP IWF) built into the router acts as a PCP client. It turns each UPnP IGD request into a PCP MAP request, keeps a local mapping table, and turns the PCP answers back into UPnP replies and error codes.
tldr.outcome: UPnP applications keep working unchanged behind a PCP-controlled NAT. The function cannot tell the local control point about later failures, such as a failed renewal or a changed external address.

today: RFC 6970 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6887 and leaves open how to handle a failing renewal and how to coexist with a PCP Proxy.

sections.title: Why an Interworking Function
sections.content:
The Port Control Protocol (PCP, RFC 6887) lets a client control NAT features on devices such as a Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) AFTR or a NAT64. Many home networks, however, use a UPnP Internet Gateway Device (IGD) so that local hosts can ask the router for port mappings. Where both exist, RFC 6970 says an interworking function between UPnP IGD and PCP is required in the IGD.

Two configurations are covered: no NAT in the IGD, which is required for example in DS-Lite or NAT64 deployments, and a NAT embedded in the IGD. The function keeps a local table of all active mappings created by internal control points, which limits how many PCP messages go to the PCP server. Deciding when to turn the function off and rely on PCP only, and coexistence with a PCP Proxy, are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The router needs a translator so that your gadgets, who speak UPnP, can talk to the provider's equipment, which speaks PCP.

sections.title: The Architecture Model
sections.content:
In the usual UPnP model, an IGD Control Point or a client on the local network talks to the IGD, which is typically a NAT or firewall facing a remote host. That model breaks when PCP controls a Carrier Grade NAT (also called a Provider NAT) while internal hosts keep using UPnP IGD.

In the updated model the IGD contains all UPnP IGD server functions, a PCP client and the IGD-PCP IWF. The LAN side speaks UPnP IGD and the external side speaks PCP. If the IGD also embeds a NAT there are two NATs in the path (NAT1 in the IGD, NAT2 in the provider network). Without the IWF, the control point would get an external address and port assigned by the IGD only, with limited scope that cannot be used to reach hosts beyond NAT2. The IWF generates a well-formed PCP message from a received UPnP IGD message and the other way round.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes there are two doormen in a row, one at your house and one at the provider. The translator makes sure the outside world is told about the second doorman's door, not just the first one's.

sections.title: Mapping UPnP Variables and Methods to PCP
sections.content:
The RFC gives three tables: state variables, methods and errors. For variables, ExternalPort maps to the Suggested External Port field of a MAP message, InternalPort to the Internal Port field, PortMappingProtocol to the Protocol field (UPnP IGD supports only TCP and UDP), RemoteHost to the Remote Peer IP Address of the FILTER option, and InternalClient to the Internal IP Address of the THIRD_PARTY option. PortMappingEnabled accepts only the value 1, because PCP cannot deactivate a dynamic NAT mapping, and the IWF MUST return an error for any other value. A mapping description is relayed only if the local PCP client supports a description option.

For methods, AddPortMapping() and AddAnyPortMapping() become a MAP request. DeletePortMapping() and DeletePortMappingRange() become MAP requests with the Requested Lifetime set to 0. GetSpecificPortMappingEntry() becomes a MAP request with the PREFER_FAILURE option, preferably with a short lifetime such as 60 seconds. GetGenericPortMappingEntry() and GetListOfPortMappings() are answered locally from the IWF's table. GetExternalIPAddress() can be learned from any active mapping; if there is none, the IWF MAY request a short-lived mapping, for example to the Discard service (TCP/9 or UDP/9).
sections.plainLanguage: Each question in the home language has a matching question in the provider's language. Some questions, like "what have I already asked for?", the translator answers from its own notebook.

sections.title: Translating Errors
sections.content:
Each PCP result code has a UPnP error. Most map to 501 ActionFailed, including UNSUPP_VERSION, MALFORMED_REQUEST, UNSUPP_OPCODE, UNSUPP_OPTION, MALFORMED_OPTION, NETWORK_FAILURE, UNSUPP_PROTOCOL, ADDRESS_MISMATCH and EXCESSIVE_REMOTE_PEERS. NOT_AUTHORIZED becomes 718 ConflictInMappingEntry for IGD:1 and 606 Action not authorized for IGD:2.

NO_RESOURCES and USER_EX_QUOTA become 501 for IGD:1 and 728 NoPortMapsAvailable for IGD:2, and the two cannot be told apart. CANNOT_PROVIDE_EXTERNAL becomes 718 ConflictInMappingEntry when adding a mapping, or 714 NoSuchEntryInArray when the request concerned a deletion. The RFC notes that AddPortMapping() cannot be implemented without PREFER_FAILURE, which a PCP server is not required to support.
sections.plainLanguage: When the provider says no, the translator picks the closest matching "no" that the home gadget knows how to understand.

sections.title: Creating and Finding Mappings
sections.content:
If the IGD has a NAT, the IWF MUST rewrite requests so that the internal address and port are the ones assigned by that NAT (after NAT1), and it fixes the responses on the way back so the control point sees its own internal values. The external address and port are not altered. The lifetime of a mapping in the IGD SHOULD be the one assigned by the PCP server and MUST NOT be lower.

For AddAnyPortMapping(), the IWF sends a MAP request with the requested port as a suggestion and returns whatever port the server assigned. For AddPortMapping(), which asks for a specific port, the IWF MUST add the PREFER_FAILURE option so the server fails instead of picking another port. If the port is taken, the server answers CANNOT_PROVIDE_EXTERNAL. For a short-lifetime error the IWF MAY retry after 30 seconds; the default maximum retry limit is 2. After that, or for a long-lifetime error, the control point receives ConflictInMappingEntry and may try another port.

For GetSpecificPortMappingEntry(), the IWF first checks whether the requesting control point already uses that external port and, if so, returns the entry. Otherwise it sends a short-lived MAP request with PREFER_FAILURE. If the server creates the mapping, the port was free, and the IWF answers NoSuchEntryInArray.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for a specific door number and it is taken, the translator says so and you can ask for another number. If you do not mind which door, the provider just picks one for you.

sections.title: Deleting Mappings and Lifetimes
sections.content:
On DeletePortMapping() or DeletePortMappingRange(), the IWF first checks its local table. If nothing matches, it answers at once with 714 NoSuchEntryInArray or 730 PortMappingNotFound respectively. If something matches, it sends one PCP MAP request per mapping with Requested Lifetime 0, then removes the entry from its table after a positive answer. For a range delete, the IWF MAY answer positively without waiting for all PCP answers.

Lifetimes do not line up. IGD:2 caps the lease at 604800 seconds, while PCP allows up to 4294967296 seconds. For an infinite request the IWF MUST set the PCP lifetime to 4294967296, and it MUST keep its own timer for the originally requested duration, renewing the PCP mapping periodically until that timer ends. Renewal answers are not relayed to the control point, so a failed renewal cannot be reported to it.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator keeps a notebook of every door it has asked for. It also keeps asking to renew the doors that should stay open for a long time, even though the provider only hands out short leases.

sections.title: Recovery and Changes
sections.content:
When the IWF runs on the same device as the DHCP server, its state MUST follow the DHCP state: if an internal host's address expires or is released, the IWF MUST delete all mappings bound to that address. If the external IP address changes, the IWF MAY renew the mappings it stores, which works only if it keeps a full state table. The IWF has no way to tell internal control points about a new external address or port, and stale mappings stay on the PCP server until their lifetime expires. The RFC warns that protocols sensitive to address changes, such as TCP, will be disrupted.

On an unsolicited ANNOUNCE from the server, the IWF re-installs its mappings with MAP requests that carry PREFER_FAILURE. All mappings SHOULD be kept in permanent storage, although IGD:2 itself does not require surviving a reboot.
sections.plainLanguage: If the provider changes your address, the translator can ask for the same doors again, but it has no way to tell your gadgets that the numbers moved.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IGD:2 access control and authorization levels SHOULD be applied by default. Acting on behalf of a third party SHOULD be allowed only with authentication and authorization under IGD:2, and SHOULD NOT be allowed when only IGD:1 is available.

Because the IWF creates PCP mappings for other devices of the same subscriber using THIRD_PARTY, protections from RFC 6887 must be enabled. THIRD_PARTY MUST NOT be enabled unless the network carrying the PCP messages is fully trusted, for example by access control lists on the client, the server and the path between them. Since a control point can create many mappings quickly, a port quota or similar means SHOULD be enabled to avoid exhausting port resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Not everyone in the house should be able to open doors for everyone else, and nobody should be able to grab all the door numbers, so there are limits.
